Which of the following is a coordinating conjunction?
'And' joins words or clauses of equal grammatical rank, so it is a coordinating conjunction.
Which of the following is a subordinating conjunction?
'Because' introduces a dependent clause and is therefore a subordinating conjunction.
Which of the following pairs is a correlative conjunction?
Correlative conjunctions work in pairs; 'either...or' is one such pair.
In the sentence 'Although he was tired, he finished the work', the word 'although' expresses:
'Although' introduces a concessive clause and shows contrast between two ideas.
In which sentence does 'while' express contrast rather than time?
A) While I was cooking, the phone rang.
B) While he is rich, he lives simply.
C) While she slept, the rain stopped.
D) While they walked, they talked.
E) While I read, he wrote.
In option B, 'while' contrasts wealth with a simple lifestyle; in the other options it refers to time.
She was tired, ___ she continued working until midnight.
'But' is used to join two contrasting ideas.
He studied hard, ___ he passed the examination with distinction.
'So' introduces the result of the action mentioned in the first clause.
You can pay ___ by cash ___ by card at the counter.
'Either...or' presents two alternatives from which one may be chosen.
___ my brother ___ my sister lives in Pune; both settled there years ago.
'Neither...nor' gives a negative sense, and with two singular subjects the verb agrees with the nearer one ('sister lives').
Not only the students ___ the teacher was present at the seminar.
The fixed correlative pair is 'not only...but also'.
___ did he apologise, ___ he also offered to pay for the damage.
'Not only...but also' is used here with inversion after the negative adverbial 'not only'.
___ you apologise sincerely, I will not speak to you again.
'Unless' introduces the condition under which the main clause will not happen.
Wait here ___ I return from the meeting.
'Until' indicates the point in time up to which an action continues.
___ it was raining heavily, the match continued without interruption.
'Although' introduces a concessive clause showing contrast.
He could not attend the meeting ___ he was unwell.
'Because' introduces the reason for the action in the main clause.
___ the teacher was explaining the topic, the students took notes.
'While' introduces an action happening at the same time as another.
Ravi is an engineer, ___ his brother is a doctor.
'Whereas' is used to contrast two parallel facts.
He is slow ___ steady, and his work is always accurate.
The idiom 'slow but steady' uses 'but' to contrast two qualities.
He will not come ___ you invite him personally.
'Unless' means 'if not', which fits the conditional meaning here.
___ you work hard, you will succeed in the examination.
'If' introduces the condition that leads to success.
He is not only a good singer ___ a fine dancer.
The correlative pair 'not only...but also' must be completed by 'but also'.
Neither the manager nor the employees ___ willing to accept the proposal.
With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject; 'employees' is plural, so 'were' is correct.
Either the students or the teacher ___ responsible for this mistake.
With 'either...or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject; 'teacher' is singular, so 'is' is correct.
Not only the players but also the coach ___ satisfied with the result.
With 'not only...but also', the verb agrees with the nearer subject; 'coach' is singular.
Both the sisters ___ fond of classical music.
'Both...and' joins two subjects and takes a plural verb.
Neither of the answers ___ correct, so the question was cancelled.
'Neither of' is treated as singular and takes a singular verb.
Although he was tired, (A)/ but he completed (B)/ the work (C)/ on time. (D)/ No error (E)
'Although' and 'but' both mark contrast, so using them together is redundant; remove 'but'.
Neither he (A)/ nor his friends (B)/ was present (C)/ at the meeting. (D)/ No error (E)
With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'friends', so 'were' is required.
Because he was ill, (A)/ so he did not (B)/ come to the office (C)/ yesterday. (D)/ No error (E)
'Because' already introduces the reason, so 'so' is redundant and should be removed.
Unless you do not work hard, (A)/ you will not (B)/ be able to (C)/ clear the examination. (D)/ No error (E)
'Unless' already carries a negative meaning, so 'do not' creates a double negative; use 'Unless you work hard'.
Hardly had I reached (A)/ the station (B)/ than it started (C)/ raining heavily. (D)/ No error (E)
Either of the two plans (A)/ are acceptable (B)/ to the committee (C)/ at this stage. (D)/ No error (E)
'Either of' is singular, so the verb should be 'is acceptable'.
Not only he is (A)/ a doctor (B)/ but also a writer (C)/ of great repute. (D)/ No error (E)
After 'not only' at the beginning of a clause, inversion is required: 'Not only is he'.
Combine the sentences, beginning with 'Although': He was tired. He finished the work.
A) Although he was tired, he finished the work.
B) Although he was tired, but he finished the work.
C) Although he was tired, so he finished the work.
D) Although he was tired, and he finished the work.
E) Although he was tired, or he finished the work.
'Although' alone introduces the concessive clause; adding 'but', 'so', 'and' or 'or' is incorrect.
Combine the sentences, beginning with 'Unless': Study hard. You will fail otherwise.
A) Unless you study hard, you will fail.
B) Unless you study hard, you will not fail.
C) Unless you do not study hard, you will fail.
D) Unless you studied hard, you will fail.
E) Unless you will study hard, you will fail.
'Unless' means 'if not', so the correct combination is 'Unless you study hard, you will fail'.
You cannot enter the examination hall ___ you show your identity card.
'Unless' introduces the condition that must be met before entering.
___ you like it or not, you must follow the rules of the institution.
The fixed pattern is 'whether...or not', which presents two alternatives.
Scarcely had he entered the room ___ the lights went out.
The teacher spoke slowly ___ the students could follow her explanation.
'So that' introduces a clause of purpose.
